## Results

### Recovery of regional spectral organisation on uncorrected spectra

We first tested whether the regional spectral organisation of the iEEG atlas was preserved in source-reconstructed HD-EEG, before any aperiodic correction.

#### K-means clusterisation {#result-clusterisation}

We ran the clustering on the iEEG atlas in two configurations, with and without the 0.5-80 Hz bandpass filter (Methods), to check how far our deviation from @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial accounted for differences from the published result. With the bandpass applied, the procedure recovered the eight-group structure of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial: a no-peak group plus seven peak groups, in the low delta, high delta, theta, alpha, low beta, high beta, and gamma bands. Without the bandpass it yielded seven groups: a no-peak group, two delta clusters, one theta cluster, two alpha clusters, and one beta cluster, with no gamma group and no low/high beta split (@fig-clusters B). We carried the unfiltered solution forward, because it was based on undistorted spectra, and retained the 50% of channels closest to its no-peak group as the no-peak reference set for all subsequent peak-detection tests.

The same procedure applied to the HD-EEG source-reconstructed data yielded 11 groups, with a different structure. Seven clusters had a peak in the alpha range (8-12 Hz) and differed only in peak amplitude, so the clustering over-segmented a single alpha-dominated continuum rather than resolving distinct bands (@fig-clusters C). No distinct theta or beta clusters emerged (the band labels along the top axis are frequency guides, not cluster identities), and the sharp notch at 50 Hz reflects line-noise removal. The HD-EEG no-peak cluster was flatter than its iEEG counterpart.

We labelled each cluster by its "band peak frequency", the frequency at which its spectrum showed the maximum deviation from the no-peak baseline; this is meaningful only where a cluster carries a genuine peak. In HD-EEG, only the $\delta$ and $\alpha$ clusters showed a clear bump above the aperiodic background. The remaining high-frequency clusters were separated by a shallower aperiodic slope and an elevated broadband tail, not by a gamma oscillation. Whereas the iEEG atlas resolved band-specific oscillatory clusters from $\delta$ to $\gamma$, the HD-EEG structure was dominated by alpha power and aperiodic slope (@fig-ieeg-clusters).

#### Clustering stability and data driven intervals 

We next evaluated the stability of the clustering solution, the no-peak reference set, and the data-driven frequency intervals used for regional peak detection. These components were sensitive to preprocessing choices and to the fitted frequency range: small changes in the lower or upper bound altered the number of clusters and the membership and shape of the no-peak reference set. This was worst in the source-reconstructed HD-EEG data, where some configurations failed to produce a no-peak set at all.

The data-driven intervals also failed to transfer. @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial defined 22 intervals so that each held at least 4% of the total mean power in iEEG; applied to the HD-EEG spectra, the same rule yielded 21 intervals and split the range above 31.75 Hz into five separate intervals, where the atlas defined a single 31.75-80 Hz band. We attributed this gamma over-segmentation to the unit-power normalisation (see Discussion). Because the rule did not transfer, we retained the fixed 22 intervals of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial for both modalities to keep them comparable.


For this reason the 4% condition does not transfer to source-reconstructed data, and data-driven HD-EEG intervals are not directly comparable with the iEEG atlas. To preserve cross-modal comparability, the fixed 22 intervals of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial were retained for both modalities in all regional peak-detection tests (@fig-stat-reg_dfiff ).

The clustering, the no-peak reference, and the power-based interval definition were therefore potentially unstable across reasonable preprocessing choices. We did not apply this k-means descriptor to the aperiodic-corrected (`specparam`) spectra. In the subsequent analyses we instead characterised oscillatory content with the per-band parametrised-peak descriptor, which needs neither a clustering step nor a no-peak reference and was therefore less dependent on these preprocessing choices.

#### Band-power map and cross-modal overlap

We present regional relative band power, compared across modalities with the band-overlap metric.

Regional relative-power maps agreed across modalities most strongly in the alpha band (r = 0.60) and, more weakly, in the delta band (r = 0.42). Theta showed essentially no cross-modal correspondence (r = 0.13), beta only weak agreement (r = 0.30), and gamma was anti-correlated (r = −0.29). The spatial organisation of relative power is therefore only partially preserved between the iEEG atlas and source-reconstructed HD-EEG, and the preservation is band-dependent: it is confined largely to the alpha and low-frequency ranges that carry the clearest oscillatory structure, and breaks down at high frequencies. The negative gamma correlation is consistent with the high-frequency HD-EEG signal being dominated by a shallow aperiodic tail and noise floor rather than by physiological gamma — the same mechanism that drove the spurious gamma over-segmentation in the interval analysis — so that regions ranked high in HD-EEG gamma relative power are not those ranked high in the atlas. Relative to the identity line

These per-band correlations should be read as descriptive rather than inferential. Relative band powers are *compositional*: within each channel they are normalised to a fixed total, so the five bands are not independent and an increase in one band necessarily depresses the others. This closure constraint induces negative coupling between bands by construction — part of the negative gamma correlation is therefore arithmetic rather than physiological — and it violates the independence assumptions of ordinary correlation and t-tests applied to the raw proportions[@filzmoser2012CorrelationAnalysisCompositional]. Valid inference would require analysing the maps in a log-ratio space (e.g. centred or isometric log-ratio transforms), which also removes any dependence on the per-channel normalisation choice. We retain the untransformed maps here as a descriptive summary and defer formal cross-modal inference to the aperiodic-separated peak descriptors below, which are not subject to the same closure.

### Periodic/aperiodic separation

#### Presence-gated overlap {#sec-presence-gated}

The band-overlap metric scores cross-modal *agreement* alone, and presupposes that a rhythm is present: two flat residuals agree trivially, so a high overlap can mean the two modalities share an oscillation or that neither carries one. We separated these by gating the aperiodic-removed overlap on an explicit presence test. For each region and band we bootstrapped the mean oscillatory-residual power, resampling whole subjects (iEEG patients, HD-EEG datasets; 2000 resamples), and called a cell *present* when its 95% CI excluded zero. We gated on the iEEG atlas as the reference: where iEEG carries no detectable rhythm the overlap is uninterpretable, and where it does we ask whether HD-EEG recovers it (@fig-overlap-gated).

The gate removes much of the map from interpretation. Of the 190 region × band cells, 57 (30%) carry no bootstrap-significant iEEG rhythm — most of theta (26 of 38 regions) and over half of alpha's (20) — and their overlap is vacuous whatever its value. Of the 133 cells where iEEG does carry a rhythm, HD-EEG recovers it in only 79 (59%); the remaining 54 are iEEG-present but HD-absent. The failures are band-structured: HD recovers every region's alpha (18 of 18, none missed) but misses most of the high-frequency rhythms iEEG carries — 20 of 31 gamma and 18 of 37 delta cells are HD-absent — and where both modalities are present the agreement is highest in beta (median overlap 0.68) and lowest in gamma (0.39). The high-frequency cross-modal "agreement" of the ungated metric is therefore largely an *absence* of recoverable HD-EEG rhythm rather than a shared one, consistent with the noise-floor account of the HD gamma tail.

![Presence-gated cross-modal overlap on the aperiodic-removed residual. A region × band cell is grey where the iEEG atlas has no bootstrap-significant oscillatory power (overlap uninterpretable), marked × where iEEG carries a rhythm that HD-EEG does not recover (its residual-power 95% CI includes zero), and coloured by the Afnan overlap only where both modalities are present. Presence is a subject-clustered bootstrap (whole subjects resampled — iEEG patients, HD datasets; 2000 resamples).](figures/chapter2/corrected/afnan_overlap_corrected_presence_gated_heatmap.svg){#fig-overlap-gated width="60%"}


#### Per-band peak prevalence from specparam

Once oscillations are modelled explicitly, peak prevalence — the fraction of a region's channels carrying at least one fitted peak in a band — diverges sharply between modalities (@fig-peak-prevalence). Source HD-EEG is dominated by alpha: mean prevalence across regions is 0.63 in alpha but only 0.11 in theta, 0.05 in gamma and 0.01 in delta. The iEEG atlas is broader, with substantial beta (0.40), gamma (0.26) and alpha (0.24) prevalence. The difference map (HD − iEEG) is strongly positive in alpha — HD detects alpha peaks far more often, especially in posterior regions — and negative across beta and gamma, where iEEG detects high-frequency peaks that the source fit does not recover.

Cross-modal agreement of the regional prevalence *pattern* (Spearman across the 38 bilateral regions) is confined to the low and mid bands: alpha $\rho = 0.60$ and beta $\rho = 0.47$, against delta $\rho = 0.04$, theta $\rho = -0.07$ and gamma $\rho = -0.25$ (@fig-prevalence-scatter). In alpha the points sit above the identity line — HD detects alpha in more regions than iEEG — yet the two modalities still rank regions consistently. This mirrors the uncorrected relative-band-power result (alpha strongest, gamma anti-correlated), now with the aperiodic background modelled out rather than carried in the power.

Because modelled power exists only where a peak is fitted, prevalence is also the peak-detection rate and must be read alongside the amplitude and centre-frequency descriptors. Mean peaks per channel were similar across modalities (iEEG 1.45, HD 1.37 under the main settings), but 99.7% of iEEG channels passed the $R^2 > 0.9$ screen against only 74.0% of HD channels, with the missing HD peaks concentrated in the high-frequency bands where the source spectrum is flattest.

**Modelled power.** <!-- REVIEW: "tells the same story in amplitude that prevalence tells in detection" — LLM-style parallelism/cliché. State the finding directly. -->
The amplitude of the highest peak per band (median across the channels that carry a peak) tells the same story in amplitude that prevalence tells in detection: posterior alpha carries the largest modelled power in HD-EEG, while in iEEG the amplitude is spread across beta in frontal and central regions (@fig-modelled-power).

![Modelled band power by region and modality: median amplitude (log-power height above the aperiodic component) of the highest peak in each band, over channels with a detected peak.](figures/chapter2/peaks/modelled_power_heatmap.svg){#fig-modelled-power width="100%" column="page"}

**Centre frequency and dominant rhythm.** Because canonical-band assignment is sensitive to peaks near a band edge, we also examined the fitted centre frequencies directly. The HD-EEG centre-frequency distribution is a sharp alpha mode at ~10 Hz, sitting squarely against the 8 and 13 Hz band edges, whereas iEEG peaks are broadly distributed with an additional high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz (@fig-centre-freq). The per-region dominant peak frequency — the centre frequency of the single highest-amplitude peak — is alpha-locked across almost all regions in HD-EEG but scatters into beta and gamma for several frontal and temporal regions in iEEG (@fig-dominant-dumbbell). The full per-region distribution of peak frequencies confirms a narrow posterior alpha ridge in HD against broader, multimodal iEEG ridges (@fig-region-ridges).

![Distribution of fitted peak centre frequencies per modality, against the canonical band edges (dashed). HD-EEG shows a single sharp ~10 Hz alpha mode; iEEG is broad with a high-gamma cluster.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_centre_frequency_distribution.svg){#fig-centre-freq width="80%"}

![Dominant peak frequency per region: the centre frequency of the highest-amplitude peak, connecting iEEG (blue) and source HD-EEG (red) for each region. Regions follow the lobe order and colouring of the heatmaps.](figures/chapter2/peaks/dominant_frequency_dumbbell.svg){#fig-dominant-dumbbell width="70%"}

![Per-region distribution of peak centre frequencies (histogram ridgeline, normalised per region), filled by lobe. HD-EEG (right) is a narrow posterior alpha ridge; iEEG (left) is broader and multimodal.](figures/chapter2/peaks/region_frequency_ridges.svg){#fig-region-ridges width="100%" column="page"}

Pooling all regions, <!-- REVIEW: "makes the contrast immediate" — LLM flourish. Cut or replace with neutral "shows". -->
the joint distribution of peak amplitude and centre frequency (@fig-size-freq) makes the contrast immediate: HD-EEG peaks form one dense high-amplitude alpha mode at ~10 Hz with a sparse low-amplitude tail above it, whereas iEEG peaks spread along the frequency axis at moderate amplitude, with a distinct beta/low-gamma body and a high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz.

![Peak size (amplitude) vs centre frequency, binned density per modality (all regions pooled). HD-EEG is a single high-amplitude alpha mode; iEEG is spread across frequency with a high-gamma cluster.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_size_vs_frequency.svg){#fig-size-freq width="100%" column="page"}

Jointly resolving peak amplitude and centre frequency per lobe (@fig-size-freq-lobe) confirms that the two descriptors are not redundant. In HD-EEG the per-channel peak density concentrates into a single tall alpha column in occipital and parietal lobes — high amplitude at ~10 Hz — and thins sharply elsewhere. In iEEG the density is spread along the frequency axis at moderate amplitude, with frontal and temporal lobes carrying beta and low-gamma peaks that have no HD-EEG counterpart. Normalising to peaks per channel makes the lobes comparable despite their different channel counts, and shows the cross-modal divergence is one of *where in the spectrum* rhythms occur, not merely how strong they are.

![Peak size (amplitude) vs centre frequency, binned density per lobe (rows) and modality (columns), normalised to peaks per channel so lobes of different size are comparable. HD-EEG concentrates in a posterior alpha column; iEEG spreads across frequency, with frontal/temporal beta-gamma.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_size_vs_frequency_by_lobe.svg){#fig-size-freq-lobe width="100%" column="page"}

#### Cross-modal overlap before and after aperiodic correction

Removing the aperiodic component changes the cross-modal picture, and the change depends on how the oscillatory residual is defined. We computed the per-lobe oscillatory spectrum in 2 Hz bins under four extractors — the detrended residual and the modelled (specparam-peak) power, each in a log and a linear form — and compared modalities with a subject-clustered bootstrap (per-lobe mean ± 95% CI, @fig-residual-state) and a frequency cluster-permutation test (Maris-Oostenveld, resampling whole subjects) that controls the family-wise error across frequency (@fig-residual-diff).

The **modelled** rhythmic power — the measure that does not depend on the accuracy of the aperiodic fit — shows iEEG and HD-EEG differing in a contiguous beta/low-gamma cluster (~25-48 Hz, iEEG higher) across most lobes, and a parietal alpha cluster (~10-12 Hz) where HD-EEG is higher; occipital high-gamma is again higher in iEEG. The **detrended residual** reproduces the beta excess but adds a broad high-frequency cluster (~55-80 Hz) in which HD-EEG appears systematically higher than iEEG across every lobe. This high-frequency block is present in the residual but absent from the modelled measure, identifying it as aperiodic-tail/noise leakage rather than a rhythm — exactly the conflation that @castanheira2025QuantifyingRhythmicArrhythmic predict for detrended spectra.
<!-- REVIEW: "exactly the conflation that ... predict" overstates the match. "the kind of conflation ... describe" is safer. -->
 The log and linear residuals agree on the sign and location of the clusters but differ in magnitude, as expected from their different units.

We therefore read the modelled-peak comparison as the substantive cross-modal result: the rhythms that survive aperiodic separation correspond across modalities chiefly in the alpha band, with a beta/low-gamma offset, whereas the apparent high-frequency cross-modal difference in the subtraction residual is an artefact of the aperiodic background rather than a difference in oscillatory activity.

Lines coloured by lobe.](figures/chapter2/peaks/lobe_oscillatory_state_bootstrap.svg){#fig-residual-state width="100%" column="page"}
